preview_text: หลอดเลือดใน TCM ไม่ใช่ปัญหาท่อประปาธรรมดา แต่เป็นภาพสะท้อนของความไม่สมดุลของระบบ เช่น เสมหะ ความเมื่อยล้าของเลือด หรือการขาดสารอาหารอย่างลึกซึ้ง โดยการจัดการรูปแบบเหล่านี้ ...

synonyms: ["Artery Blockage", "Arteriosclerosis", "Artery Degeneration", "Plaque Buildup In Arteries", "Senile Arteritis", "Senile Endarteritis", "Vascular Disease"]
conventional_description: Atherosclerosis is a condition where arteries become narrowed and hardened due to a buildup of plaque - fat, cholesterol, calcium, and other substances - on the inner walls. This buildup restricts blood flow and can lead to serious complications like heart attack, stroke, or peripheral artery disease. Diagnosis typically involves blood tests to check cholesterol and inflammation markers, imaging such as ultrasound or CT scans, and sometimes angiography to see the blockages directly.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on slowing plaque progression and preventing clots. Lifestyle changes - a heart-healthy diet, exercise, and quitting smoking - are foundational. Medications commonly include statins to lower cholesterol, antihypertensives to control blood pressure, and antiplatelet drugs like aspirin to reduce clotting risk. In advanced cases, procedures such as angioplasty with stenting or bypass surgery may be needed to restore blood flow.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees atherosclerosis as a condition rooted in two main pathological accumulations: Phlegm and Blood Stagnation. When the Spleen is weak - often from poor diet, stress, or aging - it fails to transform fluids properly, and dampness condenses into thick, turbid Phlegm. This Phlegm can seep into the blood vessels and stick to the walls, forming the fatty deposits that narrow the arteries.
At the same time, if Qi flow is obstructed or deficient, blood circulation slows and congeals, creating Blood Stagnation that hardens and thickens the vessel walls.
The underlying driver is almost always a deficiency - most commonly of the Spleen and Kidney. The Spleen provides the energy to move and transform, while the Kidneys store the body's foundational Yin and Yang. As these reserves decline with age or chronic illness, the vessels lose their nourishment and elasticity, becoming dry, brittle, and more susceptible to damage. This is why atherosclerosis is more common in older adults and those with long-standing metabolic imbalance.
Because the root is deficiency and the branch is excess (Phlegm, Stagnation, sometimes Heat), the same Western diagnosis can present very differently in different people. One person may have a heavy, sluggish feeling with a greasy tongue coating (Phlegm dominant), while another has sharp, fixed chest pain and a purple tongue (Blood Stagnation dominant), and a third may feel profoundly fatigued with a weak pulse (Qi Deficiency). Each requires a fundamentally different treatment strategy.
classical_quote: 「胸痹不得卧，心痛彻背者，栝蒌薤白半夏汤主之。」
classical_translation: "Chest impediment with inability to lie flat and pain penetrating to the back is treated with Gualou Xiebai Banxia Tang. This describes a condition of phlegm-turbidity obstructing the chest, which closely mirrors the pathophysiology of atherosclerotic plaque in the coronary arteries."

tcm_diagnosis:
When a TCM practitioner sees atherosclerosis, they look beyond the plaque itself to the underlying imbalances that allowed it to form. They ask about energy, digestion, mood, and the exact nature of any pain, and they pay close attention to the tongue and pulse. These details help them identify which pattern is driving the vessel changes.
If the person tends to be overweight, feels chest oppression, produces a lot of phlegm, and has a greasy tongue coating with a slippery pulse, the pattern is likely Phlegm. This turbid, damp accumulation is considered the main building material of the plaque.
When sharp, fixed, stabbing pain is the dominant complaint, and the tongue looks dark purple with stasis spots while the pulse feels choppy or wiry, Blood Stagnation is the key pattern. The blood is not moving smoothly, and that stagnation hardens and thickens the vessel walls.
If fatigue and weakness are prominent, the complexion is pale or sallow, and the pain is dull rather than sharp, the problem may be Qi Deficiency causing Blood Stagnation. The tongue may be pale with dark spots, and the pulse is weak and deep. Here the blood stagnates because the Qi is too weak to push it along.
When the phlegm pattern turns hot, you get Phlegm-Heat. The person may feel chest fullness with a burning sensation, have a dry mouth, bad breath, and a yellow greasy tongue coating with a rapid, slippery pulse. The heat makes the plaque more inflammatory and unstable.
If the person is thin, tired, has a dry mouth but doesn’t want to drink much, and the tongue is red or pale with little coating, the pattern is Qi and Yin Deficiency. The vessels lack proper nourishment, and the blood becomes sluggish due to the dryness and weakness.
In older adults, Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency often underlies atherosclerosis. They may complain of dizziness, tinnitus, sore lower back, and dry eyes. The tongue is red with scant coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. The Yin deficiency leaves the vessels dry and brittle, making plaque more likely.

patterns.symptoms: ["Chest heaviness and oppression", "Productive cough with white sticky sputum", "Heavy, sluggish feeling in the body and limbs", "Loose, sticky stools", "Mental fogginess or excessive sleepiness"]
patterns.worse_with: Damp, humid weather, Greasy, fried, or fatty foods, Dairy products, Overeating, Sedentary lifestyle, Cold, raw foods
patterns.better_with: Warm, dry weather, Light, cooked meals, Gentle exercise (walking, tai chi, etc.)
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak and fails to transform fluids, dampness accumulates and condenses into thick, turbid phlegm. This phlegm can seep into the blood vessels, where it congeals and sticks to the vessel walls, forming the fatty plaques of atherosclerosis. The result is a feeling of heaviness, chest oppression, and sluggish circulation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: swollen pale body with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating, moist. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá), like beads rolling under the fingers.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm is formed when the Spleen fails to transform fluids, often due to a diet heavy in greasy, dairy, and cold foods, or a damp living environment. These factors overwhelm the Spleen, creating more dampness that congeals into phlegm. Warmth, light meals, and movement all help the Spleen function better, promoting the transformation and excretion of dampness. Avoiding phlegm-producing foods and staying active are essential to prevent phlegm from accumulating and clogging the vessels.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and dairy-rich foods, as well as cold and raw items, which all promote dampness and phlegm. Eat warm, cooked meals with plenty of vegetables and moderate amounts of lean protein. Gentle daily exercise like walking or tai chi helps move Qi and transform phlegm. Keep living spaces dry and well-ventilated.

patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise (walking, tai chi, etc.), Warmth (warm drinks, heating pad), Stress reduction, Massage or acupressure
patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi flow is obstructed, blood cannot circulate smoothly. Over time, the sluggish blood congeals and deposits in the vessel walls, much like silt settling in a slow-moving river. This leads to the hardening and narrowing of arteries, producing the fixed, stabbing pain and dark complexion characteristic of blood stasis in atherosclerosis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) like a knife scraping bamboo, or wiry (弦 xián) when Qi stagnation is present.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis arises when Qi stagnates or cold congeals the blood. Stress tightens the Liver Qi, which then fails to propel blood, while cold physically thickens blood and slows its flow. Gentle movement, warmth, and relaxation all encourage Qi to move and blood to circulate, preventing the stasis that leads to plaque buildup.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Warm the body and move the blood. Include warming spices like turmeric, ginger, and garlic in meals. Eat moderate amounts of onion, chives, and eggplant. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which congeal blood. Gentle daily exercise-walking, tai chi, or cycling-keeps circulation active. Do not sit for long periods; take short movement breaks.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi is deficient, it lacks the strength to push blood through the vessels. This sluggish flow allows blood to congeal and form stasis, which over time deposits as plaque on artery walls. The result is a combination of deep fatigue and fixed, stabbing pain - the hallmark of atherosclerosis driven by Qi deficiency with blood stasis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-dark or pale-purple body, possible stasis spots, teeth marks, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: deep, fine or weak, and choppy.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi deficiency means the body lacks the energy to push blood; overexertion further drains Qi, allowing stasis to worsen. Cold and raw foods chill the Spleen, impairing Qi production, while a sedentary lifestyle slows Qi and blood circulation, encouraging plaque buildup. Rest, gentle movement, and warm nourishing meals restore Qi and keep blood moving, directly countering the root deficiency and its stasis consequence.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, and easily digestible foods like congee, stews, and steamed vegetables with small amounts of lean meat. Avoid cold, raw, or greasy foods that further weaken digestion. Gentle daily movement such as walking, tai chi, or qigong helps Qi circulate and prevents blood from stagnating. Prioritize rest and avoid overexertion.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the body fails to transform fluids properly, they accumulate as phlegm. Over time, this phlegm can become stagnant and generate heat, creating a sticky, inflammatory mixture that deposits inside the arteries. This Phlegm-Heat makes the vessel walls thick and inflamed, contributing directly to plaque buildup and a sense of chest oppression or burning.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, may be slightly swollen, with a thick yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Heat arises from excess Dampness and Heat in the body. Greasy, spicy, and alcoholic foods add more Dampness and Heat, directly thickening the phlegm and inflaming the vessels. Cooling, light foods and herbs like peppermint clear Heat, while gentle movement keeps Qi and fluids circulating so phlegm cannot settle. Stress and anger stir up internal Heat, so staying calm helps prevent the pattern from flaring.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods, as well as alcohol, which all generate more Phlegm and Heat. Favor cooling, light foods like cucumber, pear, and mung beans. Gentle daily movement such as walking helps Qi flow and keeps phlegm from stagnating.

patterns.why_this_happens: Qi is the engine that moves blood and nourishes the vessel walls. When Qi is weak, blood flow slows and becomes stagnant. Yin is the cooling, moisturizing force; when it is depleted, the vessel walls become dry, brittle, and prone to damage. This combination of sluggish flow and fragile vessels allows fatty deposits to accumulate, forming atherosclerotic plaques. Over time, the body’s lack of energy and moisture deepens the damage.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red or pale-red body with thin or no coating, possibly cracked and dry. Pulse: fine (thin), weak, and often rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Yin are depleted, so anything that further drains energy or dries fluids worsens the condition. Rest and gentle movement conserve Qi, while moistening foods and cool environments replenish Yin and soothe the Empty Heat that arises from Yin deficiency.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, moistening foods like congee, yams, pears, and black sesame. Avoid spicy, fried, or overly dry foods that deplete fluids. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork; gentle movement such as Tai Chi or walking can strengthen Qi without draining it. Keep the living environment cool and humidified to soothe Yin deficiency.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Kidney and Liver Yin are depleted, the body's nourishing fluids run dry. The blood vessels lose their moisture and elasticity, becoming stiff and brittle. This dryness, combined with the low-grade heat from Yin deficiency, damages the vessel walls and makes them more susceptible to plaque buildup and hardening.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine (thin), rapid, and often wiry; the left Chi (Kidney) position is weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Liver Yin are easily consumed by overwork, stress, and heat. Rest and cooling, moist foods replenish Yin fluids, while acupuncture and herbs directly nourish the depleted essence. Avoiding stimulants and hot environments prevents further fluid loss, allowing the vessels to regain some elasticity and resilience.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Emphasize moist, cooling foods like black sesame, goji berries, mulberries, and pears. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods as well as alcohol and coffee, which deplete Yin. Gentle exercise like tai chi and adequate sleep help conserve Yin. Manage stress to prevent further Liver Yin depletion.

formulas.description: A classical formula for chest pain that radiates to the back, difficulty breathing, and inability to lie flat, caused by phlegm blocking the chest. Originally recorded by Zhang Zhongjing for a condition called 'chest obstruction,' it works by clearing away accumulated phlegm, restoring warmth and openness to the chest, and directing Qi downward. In modern practice it is most commonly used alongside conventional treatment for coronary heart disease and angina.

It builds on the famous Si Wu Tang (Four-Substance Decoction) by adding Peach Kernel and Safflower to strengthen its ability to move stagnant Blood and promote healthy circulation.

formulas.description: A classical formula designed to improve blood circulation in the chest, relieve pain, and ease emotional tension. It is widely used for chronic chest pain, stubborn headaches, insomnia, and irritability caused by poor blood flow and stagnation in the upper body.

formulas.description: A classical four-herb formula designed to replenish the body's fundamental vitality. It addresses deep fatigue, weakness, poor appetite, sensitivity to cold, and general depletion by strengthening the Qi of the Lungs, Spleen, and Kidneys. Originally used in pediatric care, it is now widely applied to many conditions involving profound Qi deficiency.

formulas.translation: Coptis Gallbladder-Warming Decoction · Qīng dynasty, 1868 CE

formulas.description: A classical formula used to clear Heat and resolve Phlegm that is disturbing the mind and digestive system. It is commonly used for insomnia, restlessness, nausea, and a bitter taste in the mouth caused by the accumulation of Phlegm-Heat in the Gallbladder and Stomach. Think of it as a formula that calms both an agitated mind and an upset stomach by addressing the underlying combination of inflammatory Heat and sticky Phlegm.

formulas.translation: Generate the Pulse Powder · Jīn dynasty, ~1186 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Tonifies Qi, Generates Fluids, Nourishes Yin
formulas.description: A classical three-herb formula used to restore vitality when both Qi and body fluids have been depleted. It addresses fatigue, shortness of breath, excessive sweating, dry throat, and weak pulse caused by heat exhaustion, chronic illness, or prolonged coughing that has weakened the Lungs. In modern practice, it is also widely used as supportive treatment for heart conditions including heart failure and irregular heartbeat.

formulas.description: A classical formula for deep exhaustion and weakness caused by deficiency of both Qi and Blood, particularly when the Spleen, Lungs, and Heart are all depleted. It is used for people who feel chronically tired, have poor appetite, palpitations, forgetfulness, trouble sleeping, dry throat and lips, hair loss, and a generally frail constitution. It works by strongly replenishing Qi and Blood while calming the mind and spirit.

formulas.translation: Restore the Left Pill · Míng dynasty, ~1624 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Nourishes Kidney Yin, Benefits Essence and Fills the Marrow, Nourishes Blood
formulas.description: A classical formula designed to deeply nourish Kidney Yin and replenish the body's vital essence and marrow. It is used when there is significant depletion of the body's fundamental nourishing fluids and substances, leading to symptoms such as dizziness, lower back and knee weakness, night sweats, dry mouth and throat, and a general state of thinning or exhaustion. Unlike milder Yin-nourishing formulas, Zuo Gui Wan is a purely replenishing formula without any draining ingredients, making it suitable for more severe deficiency.

It is best known for treating a condition called 'yin fei,' which involves difficulty speaking and weakness or paralysis of the legs, commonly seen after stroke or in age-related decline. The formula works on the root problem (deep Kidney weakness) and the surface symptom (phlegm blocking the brain and speech) at the same time.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture and herbs actually clear plaque from my arteries?
faqs.answer: Research and clinical experience suggest that TCM can help stabilize plaques, reduce inflammation, and improve the body's ability to metabolize fats - which may slow or even partially reverse plaque buildup over time. Herbs that move Blood and transform Phlegm, combined with acupuncture to improve circulation, work to change the internal environment so that new plaque is less likely to form and existing deposits may gradually soften. Results vary, but many patients see improvements in blood flow and a reduction in related symptoms.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe to use alongside my statins or blood thinners?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can often be used safely alongside conventional medications, but it requires careful coordination. Some blood-moving herbs like Dang Gui, Chuan Xiong, and Tao Ren may enhance the effect of anticoagulants such as warfarin or aspirin, increasing bleeding risk. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your cardiologist about all medications and supplements you are taking. Never stop or adjust your prescribed medications without medical supervision.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM?
faqs.answer: Most people notice improvements in energy, chest comfort, and overall well-being within 4-6 weeks. Lab markers like cholesterol and blood pressure may begin to shift after 2-3 months. Significant plaque stabilization or regression is a longer process, often taking 6-12 months of consistent treatment and lifestyle changes. Your TCM practitioner will monitor your progress through symptom changes and tongue/pulse assessment, adjusting your formula as your pattern evolves.

faqs.question: What diet should I follow to support my TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: A TCM-friendly diet for atherosclerosis emphasizes warm, cooked foods that support the Spleen and reduce Phlegm and Dampness. Favor whole grains, legumes, lightly cooked vegetables, and moderate amounts of lean protein. Avoid greasy, fried, and overly sweet foods, as well as excessive dairy and cold raw foods, which weaken digestion and promote Phlegm. Small amounts of onion, garlic, turmeric, and hawthorn berry can gently support circulation.

faqs.question: Can TCM prevent a heart attack or stroke?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalances that lead to plaque formation and vessel damage, which may lower the long-term risk of heart attack and stroke. By improving blood flow, reducing inflammation, and strengthening the body's Qi and Yin, TCM works as a preventive strategy. However, it does not replace emergency medical care. If you have acute chest pain, sudden weakness, or other warning signs, seek immediate medical attention.

faqs.question: Will I need acupuncture forever?
faqs.answer: No. Acupuncture is typically most intensive at the beginning - often weekly for the first 2-3 months. As your condition stabilizes, sessions can be tapered to every other week, then monthly, and eventually to seasonal tune-ups. Herbal therapy may also be reduced or stopped once your pattern has shifted. The goal is to restore balance so that your body can maintain vascular health with minimal ongoing intervention.

research.title: Effect of Xuefu Zhuyu Decoction on carotid atherosclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled data from multiple RCTs and found that adding Xue Fu Zhu Yu Tang to standard care significantly reduced carotid intima-media thickness and improved blood lipid profiles compared to standard care alone. The study supports the formula's traditional use for Blood Stagnation-driven atherosclerosis.
research.periodical: Wang J, et al. Effect of Xuefu Zhuyu Decoction on carotid atherosclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2018;24(8):567-575.

research.title: Huanglian Wendan Decoction for phlegm-heat type atherosclerosis: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In this RCT, 120 patients with carotid atherosclerosis and a Phlegm-Heat pattern were treated with either Huang Lian Wen Dan Tang plus atorvastatin or atorvastatin alone. After 12 weeks, the combination group showed greater reductions in plaque area and inflammatory markers, with fewer gastrointestinal side effects.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Clinical study on Huanglian Wendan Decoction in treating phlegm-heat obstructing the lung type carotid atherosclerosis. Chinese Journal of Experimental Traditional Medical Formulae. 2020;26(15):112-118.

research.title: Acupuncture for stable angina pectoris: a systematic review
research.description: This review evaluated 16 RCTs and concluded that acupuncture as an adjunct to conventional medication significantly reduced angina frequency and improved exercise tolerance in patients with coronary artery disease, which is closely linked to atherosclerosis. The most commonly used points were Neiguan PC-6 and Xinshu BL-15.
research.periodical: Chen Y, et al. Acupuncture for stable angina pectoris: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2019;2019:8567127.
